sections.h: Psalms of Solomon 2 and 8: the siege and the death in Egypt
sections.b: Psalm 2 of the Psalms of Solomon mourns a conqueror who battered down Jerusalem's walls with a ram and let foreign soldiers trample the altar, then rejoices that God showed him "stabbed through on the mountains of Egypt," his body tossed on the waves with no one to bury him (Psalms of Solomon 2:1-2; 2:30-31). Psalm 8 tells how the rulers of the land welcomed "the one from the far end of the earth," and how he seized the towers, killed the leaders and led sons and daughters away (8:16-24). G. Buchanan Gray (1913) matched these details with Josephus's account of 63 BC (Antiquities 14.3-4; Jewish War 1.7) and with Pompey's murder near Mount Casius in 48 BC (Plutarch, Pompey 77-80; Cassius Dio 42.3-5), and concluded that the conqueror and Pompey "are one and the same person." Frankenberg's alternative, Antiochus IV, required reading the death in Egypt as a prophecy that never came true (as Gray reports).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:1–2; Psalms of Solomon 2:29–35; Psalms of Solomon 8:16–24

common: The dragon of Psalms of Solomon 2:29 is Pompey.
uncommon: Cheyne (1910), as Gray (1913) reports, denied that the dragon of Psalms of Solomon 2:29 is Pompey.

sections.h: Rome arrives: the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon describe the Roman army as God's instrument against a sinful Jerusalem (Psalms of Solomon 2:3-8; 8:15-17), an instrument that acted out of greed, "not out of zeal" (2:27), and they pray for God to stop the nations' cruelty (2:24-26). Josephus says the capture of 63 BC cost the Jews their liberty and made Jerusalem pay tribute to Rome (Antiquities 14.4.4-5).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:1–29; Psalms of Solomon 8:15–24

sections.h: The fall of the Hasmonean kingdom in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon describe the end of the Hasmonean state from its opponents' side: a rich and proud Jerusalem lifted "as high as the stars" (Psalms of Solomon 1:4-5), leaders who profaned the sanctuary (1:8; 8:12-13), and rulers who opened the gates to the foreign conqueror (8:18-19). Josephus tells how the brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II both appealed to Pompey, and how Hyrcanus's party let the Romans into the city while Aristobulus's party held the Temple (Antiquities 14.3-4).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 1:4–8; Psalms of Solomon 8:12–24

sections.h: The Psalms of Solomon: foreign feet on the altar
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 2:2 mourns foreign soldiers climbing God's altar in their sandals, and 8:12-13 accuses Jerusalem's own leaders of robbing the sanctuary and coming to the altar unclean. Josephus and Tacitus remember instead that Pompey went into the holy place (Josephus, Jewish War 1.7.6; Histories of Tacitus 5:9). Psalm 7 of the collection prays that God will not "take your tent away" from his people (7:1).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:2–4; Psalms of Solomon 7:1–5; Psalms of Solomon 8:12–13; Histories of Tacitus 5:9

sections.h: Jerusalem as a humbled queen (Psalms of Solomon 1-2)
sections.b: In the Psalms of Solomon Jerusalem seems to speak as a mother (the Greek of 1:3 is feminine in Swete's text) who thought herself righteous and rich in children (Psalms of Solomon 1:2-3), and is pictured as a queen stripped of her fine clothes and crown, wearing sackcloth and a rope (2:19-23), an image from Isaiah 3:24 and Lamentations 1. Baruch 5:1-2 reverses it, dressing her again in the turban of glory.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 1:1–8; Psalms of Solomon 2:19–23; Isaiah 3:24; Lamentations 1:1; Baruch 5:1–2

sections.h: A human dragon: Psalms of Solomon 2:29
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 2:29 calls the conqueror of Jerusalem "the dragon" (drakōn), as the Greek of Jeremiah 51:34 calls Nebuchadnezzar. Gray (1913) took him to be Pompey, killed in Egypt (2:30).

sections.h: "Will rise to eternal life": Psalms of Solomon 3
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 3 contrasts the sinner, who falls and "will not rise" (3:13), with those who fear the Lord, who "will rise to eternal life" in the Lord's light (3:16). It agrees with Daniel 12:2 on the righteous. If "will not rise" means that the sinner will not rise from the dead, it differs from Daniel 12:2, John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15, where the wicked rise too; the line can also mean that he never recovers from his fall.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 3:13–16; Daniel 12:2; John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Luke 14:14

sections.h: Mercy in the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: Mercy (eleos, the Greek Bible's usual word for hesed) is a key word of the Psalms of Solomon: God's mercy on those who fear him, "with judgment" (Psalms of Solomon 2:37-40), his open hand (5:14), his name dwelling among his people (7:4-5), and the closing prayer "Turn your mercy toward us" (8:33-34).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:37–40; Psalms of Solomon 5:14–17; Psalms of Solomon 7:4–5; Psalms of Solomon 8:33–34

sections.h: "The devout" of the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon call their own group hosioi, "the devout," the Greek of Hebrew hasidim (Gray, 1913), and set them against "the sinners" (Psalms of Solomon 2:40; 4:1; 8:28). Gray identified them with the Pharisees; the introduction to the Psalms of Solomon sets out the other proposals.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:40; Psalms of Solomon 4:1–9; Psalms of Solomon 8:28; 1 Maccabees 2:42

sections.h: The people-pleasers of Psalms of Solomon 4
sections.b: Gray (1913) took the hypocritical judge of Psalms of Solomon 4, "harsh in words when he condemns sinners," for a Sadducee, comparing Josephus, who calls the Sadducees "very rigid in judging offenders, above all the rest of the Jews" (Antiquities 20.9.1). The psalm itself names no party.

sections.h: The people-pleasers of the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 4 is a whole poem against a hypocrite who sits in the devout council: severe in public, adulterous and deceitful in private, telling himself "that no one sees and no one judges" (4:14). It calls such men anthrōpareskoi, "people-pleasers" (4:0), the word of Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22, and takes up the Greek of Psalm 52:6 (Psalm 53:5 in English Bibles), which says that God scattered the bones of people-pleasers; 4:21 echoes it. If the devout were Pharisees, as Gray (1913) thought, they attack the same fault Jesus later charges against some Pharisees (Matthew 23:28).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 4:1–25; Ephesians 6:6; Colossians 3:22; Psalm 53:5; Matthew 23:28

sections.h: God feeds the poor: Psalms of Solomon 5
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 5 is a poor man's hymn: God is the refuge of the poor (5:2), feeds birds, fish, kings and peoples (5:11-13), and gives a modest share with righteousness as a blessing (5:18-20). Gray (1913) noted that the book's devout were largely people of small means.

sections.h: "If a person has far too much, he sins"
sections.b: Psalms of Solomon 5:18-20 praises "a fitting measure of enough" and warns that too much leads to sin, like Proverbs 30:8-9 and 1 Timothy 6:6-8. Psalm 1 of the collection shows the rich of Jerusalem growing insolent in their good times (1:4-6).
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 5:18–20; Psalms of Solomon 1:4–6; Proverbs 30:8–9; 1 Timothy 6:6–8

sections.h: Declaring God in the right (Psalms of Solomon)
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon meet disaster by "justifying" God, declaring his judgments right (Psalms of Solomon 2:16; 3:3-5; 8:7; 8:27-32). God judges the nations but disciplines Israel (8:32), and the righteous accept his discipline (3:4; 7:3), as Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-11 teach.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:16–19; Psalms of Solomon 3:3–5; Psalms of Solomon 8:27–32; Psalm 51:4; Hebrews 12:5–11

sections.h: Headings of the Psalms of Solomon
sections.b: The Psalms of Solomon carry headings like the biblical Psalms': "A psalm of Solomon" (compare Psalm 72:0 and 127:0), "A conversation" (4:0), "In hope" (6:0), "Of turning back" (7:0), "For victory" (8:0). Swete's footnotes show the manuscripts differing over them, and Gray (1913) took "For victory" as the Greek of the Hebrew term this site renders "For the music director." Psalm 1 has no heading in Swete's text.

sections.b: After Pompey led captives to Rome (Psalms of Solomon 2:6; 8:24; Josephus, Antiquities 14.4.5), the Psalms of Solomon pray, "Gather the scattered people of Israel with mercy and kindness" (8:34), the hope of Deuteronomy 30:3-4.
sections.refs: Psalms of Solomon 2:6; Psalms of Solomon 8:24; Psalms of Solomon 8:34; Deuteronomy 30:3–4
